https://www.politico.eu/article/greece-f.text: ATHENS — As Spain and France began to gain control over devastating wildfires that last week sparked one of their largest peacetime evacuations, Greece was battling multiple blazes on Sunday — and a sense that its odyssey is far from over. Two firefighters, a Greek and a Danish national, died after a pair of helicopters battling a major wildfire burning out of control west of Athens crashed in midair. Another Greek and a British national were recovered alive. Television footage showed one of the helicopters exploding and plunging to the ground in flames after the collision. Foreign firefighting and helicopter crews are often deployed in Greece to help tackle wildfires. Advertisement Advertisement Another three Greek firefighters died last Wednesday while tackling wildfires in Crete and on the Peloponnese, a rugged peninsula in southern Greece. While a fire that has been burning since Friday around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth some 60 ​kilometers northwest of Athens has subsided, on Saturday the flames crossed a mountain to the south, fanned by strong winds of up to 130 kilometers per hour, and reached the settlement of Veniza closer to the capital. According to initial estimates, the fire has destroyed around 200 houses in the area. On Sunday flames spread rapidly through western Attica, a region that encompasses Athens, threatening communities and an industrial district outside Megara, about 30 kilometers from the capital. Speaking on state TV Ert, the president of the firefighters’ federation, Nikos Lavranos, described it as a “huge front” and a “black blanket covering an area of around [25 acres].” Dozens of settlements have been evacuated, and firefighters are focusing on preventing the flames from advancing toward Megara, pop. 30,000. Greece’s firefighting service said more than 2,500 people had been evacuated in western Attica by late Sunday afternoon. “Unfortunately, we have uncontrolled fires in far too many areas. As soon as the fire brigade arrives at one spot, just as the fire is being brought under control, it flares up again in another spot,” Megara Mayor Panagiotis Margetis told Open TV. Firefighters were also fighting another blaze in the Peloponnese on Sunday as well as on the island of Cephalonia in the Ionian Sea between Greece and Italy. More than 500 firefighters have been deployed across Greece. Advertisement Advertisement Wind speeds are set to drop significantly on Monday, according to the National Meteorological Service, which should ease the work of the fire services. Europe has been ravaged by wildfires this summer after months of record-breaking heat and little rain. Scientists have found that climate change vastly increased the likelihood of Western Europe’s record-breaking heat wave in late June as well as a spring drought — both events that made the land more fire-prone. Wildfires in France and Spain forced the evacuation of over 300,000 people last month. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis expressed his “deepest sorrow” for the “tragic accident” of the helicopters, and pledged state support for those whose homes were destroyed. “There are moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions exceed all human planning and every operational capability,” he said in a social media post on Sunday. “These are extremely difficult days for our country.”

https://hungarytoday.hu/peter-magyar-joi.text: Péter Magyar Joins “Project Ukraine,” Surrenders to the EU’s Hostile Stance towards Moscow Hungarian diplomacy has undergone a fundamental shift in its assessment of the Russian-Ukrainian war. According to a government resolution published in the Hungarian Gazette, Hungary will officially take the position at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly that Russia’s conduct represents a direct and serious threat to our country, to Europe, and to the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia. The Hungarian delegation preparing for the UN General Assembly session, which begins in September, has received a new, binding mandate from Péter Magyar. Hungary condemns Russian military aggression and fully supports the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, and recognizes Ukraine’s right to self-defense, says the prime minister’s instruction published in the Gazette. The most significant point of the resolution states that Russia’s conduct constitutes a direct threat to Hungary, Europe, and the security of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia. The radical change of course in Budapest triggered strong reactions from Russia. As Világgazdaság reported, Russian Senator Vladimir Dzhabarov criticized the decision, referring to the historical background. The Russian side also raised questions about relations in the area of energy security. Dzhabarov recalled that during World War II, Hungary attacked the Soviet Union alongside Nazi Germany, and he believes Budapest has now forgotten this historical past. He claimed that Hungary is once again attempting to revive the former grandeur of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy, as well as the era when it supported Adolf Hitler’s plans. “Well, we will take note of that,” he concluded . Vladimir Dzhabarov. Photo: council.gov.ru/Wikimedia Commons Andrey Kolesnik, a member of the Russian Duma’s Defense Committee, told Gazeta.ru that the smooth export of Russian energy supplies (oil and natural gas) to Hungary could be called into question. The politician cynically pointed out: the Hungarian government, giving in to pressure from the EU, may be forced to give up vital Russian resources. Political tensions between the two countries are being further intensified by the fact that Prime Minister Péter Magyar previously reported that an investigation had been launched in Hungary into the alleged links between former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó and Russia. The new Foreign Minister faces criticism over crisis management, diplomatic reshuffles, and a growing focus on image over tangible results. Photo courtesy of Joan Salge Blake Study Abroad Study Abroad Expo is September 9 Programs in Madrid, Singapore, and Geneva, and new offerings in Prague, to name a few September 8, 2026 Yasmine Chang Twitter Facebook For those interested in immersing themselves in a new culture, you’ll want to be sure to visit the annual Boston University Study Abroad Expo on September 9, from 10 am to 2 pm at Marsh Plaza. The event is open to all undergrads. Gareth McFeely, executive director of Study Abroad, says the expo is “one of the best opportunities for students—especially students who haven’t thought about study abroad—to learn a little bit more about what it is that we do, the range of places that we offer programs, the kinds of programs that we offer.” The expo will feature staff and ambassadors from the different cities where students can study, including Madrid, London, Singapore, Paris, and Geneva. McFeely says he’ll also be on hand to answer questions from prospective students and direct people to the appropriate tables. “I usually work at one of those tables, and I love to meet all of the students,” he says. “It’s fun.” In addition to info, there will also be free snacks and giveaways like flags and postcards. Study Abroad student ambassador Michael Vuong participated in the Sydney STEM Program in Spring 2025, where he worked at the aerospace startup Metakosmos as a mechanical engineering intern. “It got me exposed to another side of engineering that I haven’t been exposed to yet, so it [helped with my] general knowledge of manufacturing,” says Vuong (ENG’27). Apart from work, Vuong traveled to Brisbane, Melbourne, Tasmania, and New Zealand. “I think [New Zealand] was my favorite place to visit,” he says. “I remember walking out of the airplane. Instantly you can see a range of mountains, which was really memorable and beautiful. It really stuck out to me.” Nicholas Chipashvili also studied abroad and participated in the Sydney STEM Program, where he worked in a chemistry lab at the University of Sydney. He worked on creating a paint that helps capture water in the atmosphere. Through living and working abroad, Chipashvili (CAS’27) says the experience has definitely added to his personal growth. “I [gained] a lot of independence since I was basically halfway across the world, away from my parents, my friends from home, my friends from BU,” he says. “I had to make new friends, create a whole new social circle there… [I was] basically living on my own in a whole new country. It definitely built my character.” New to the study abroad city lineup this year is the Fall and Spring semester Prague program . Previously, the Prague program only offered internship opportunities for the summer term. Now, it offers both internship and academic course opportunities in the Fall, Spring, and Summer terms. Students can learn more about the expanded program at the expo. Before studying abroad, Vuong urges students to do their research. “Make sure you read through the study abroad website, and make sure you have your schedule prepared for the study abroad,” he says. He also encourages students not to consider only one program. “Maybe you’re set on one location, but after the expo, there’s another location that piques your interest,” he says. “Just be open-minded. There’s definitely a lot of options.” Event Details Boston University Study Abroad Expo This is your chance to discover all the possibilities BU Study Abroad offers and start planning. Come chat with study abroad alumni about their experiences, meet program and site staff who can answer your questions, play games, win prizes, and grab some fun swag while you explore the 150+ programs available to students.
